svg.aria-label: Diagram: the relationship between a Microsoft Entra tenant and Azure subscriptions, and the elevate access bridge between the two control planes. Microsoft Entra ID and Azure resources are secured independently: Entra role assignments do not grant access to Azure resources and Azure role assignments do not grant access to Entra. Entra roles control directory resources such as users, groups and domains; Azure roles control resources inside the subscription. Every Azure subscription trusts exactly one directory, while one tenant may be trusted by many subscriptions, and users have a single authentication home directory but can be guests in several. The single documented bridge is elevate access: a Global Administrator sets the Access management for Azure resources toggle to Yes and is assigned the User Access Administrator role at root scope, role definition ID 18d7d88d-d35e-4fb5-a5c3-7773c20a72d9, granting all read, all Microsoft.Authorization and all Microsoft.Support actions across every management group and subscription. The toggle applies only to the signed-in user and cannot be set for all Global Administrators; removal requires the same user, or PowerShell, CLI or REST. The critical trap is that with Privileged Identity Management, deactivating the Global Administrator role assignment does not change the toggle to No, so elevated Azure access persists after the time-bound directory role expires; Microsoft recommends setting the toggle to No before deactivating. Detection exists in two places: Entra directory audit logs filtered by service Azure RBAC Elevated Access, which is in preview and easier to filter and export, and Azure activity logs under Directory Activity showing Microsoft.Authorization/elevateAccess/action. A Sentinel analytics rule template named Azure RBAC Elevate Access detects it, and log reading can be delegated by assigning Reader at the scope providers/Microsoft.Insights. Portal banners warn how many users hold elevated access. Moving a subscription between directories is destructive: all Azure RBAC assignments and classic administrators lose access, role assignments are not transferred, key vaults become inaccessible until the tenant ID is changed, system-assigned managed identities must be re-enabled and user-assigned ones re-created with permissions re-established, AKS clusters lose functionality, and Azure Stack must be re-registered.
svg.title: Two control planes that do not share a model, and one narrow bridge between them
svg.text: “Microsoft Entra ID and Azure resources are secured independently from one another.”
Entra role assignments do not grant access to Azure resources. Azure role assignments do not grant access to Entra ID.
DIRECTORY PLANE — the tenant
“the directory that contains the identities used to sign in”
Entra roles control users, groups, domains.
Conditional Access · MFA · PIM for Entra roles · ID
Protection · access packages · lifecycle workflows
RESOURCE PLANE — the subscription
“the scope where Azure resources and Azure role
assignments are managed”
Azure RBAC · PIM for Azure resource roles
One directory per subscription. Many subscriptions per tenant.
no
path
… except one door, and it opens from the directory side only
Who can open it
a Global Administrator, via the “Access management for Azure resources” toggle
What it grants
User Access Administrator at ROOT SCOPE (/) — every MG and subscription
Which actions
*/read · Microsoft.Authorization/* · Microsoft.Support/* (not read-only)
Scope of the setting
per-user: “You can’t elevate access for all members of the Global Administrator role”
Removing it
same user only, or PowerShell / CLI / REST — the IAM page refuses
The leak in just-in-time privilege
“If you’re using Privileged Identity Management, deactivating your role assignment does not change the Access
management for Azure resources toggle to No.”
So a time-bound Global Admin activation can leave a PERMANENT root-scope Azure assignment behind, on a plane PIM is not watching. Toggle off BEFORE deactivating.
The detection story here is the best in the phase
Entra audit logs (preview)
Service filter: Azure RBAC (Elevated Access) — “easier to filter and export”
Azure activity log
Directory Activity → “Assigns the caller to User Access Administrator role”
Raw action
Microsoft.Authorization/elevateAccess/action
Sentinel
prebuilt analytics rule template: Azure RBAC (Elevate Access)
Delegate watching it
Reader at /providers/Microsoft.Insights — monitor without being able to do it
And the platform asks you to look, in plain language: “Action required: X users have elevated access in your tenant. You
should take immediate action and remove all role assignments with elevated access.” That count is the five-minute audit.
Moving a subscription between directories is a demolition, not a migration
All Azure RBAC assignments
“lose their access” · “aren’t transferred”
Classic administrators
Service Administrator and Co-Administrators also lose access
Key vaults
“inaccessible” until the vault tenant ID is changed
Managed identities
system-assigned re-enabled, user-assigned RE-CREATED, permissions redone
AKS · Azure Stack
cluster “loses functionality” · Azure Stack must be re-registered
So subscription-to-tenant placement is a one-time landing-zone decision. Expiry does not release it either: “the trusted
instance remains”. And the only non-elevation bridge between the planes is a GROUP an Azure role assignment references.
Sources: Elevate access to manage all Azure subscriptions and management groups, and Add an existing Azure subscription to your tenant, on Microsoft Learn.
